conflicts.contestedAction: Whether the hosted proof may fall back to the raw intake corpus bundle when oversight's vetted publication is unavailable.
conflicts.rationaleSummary: Both agents worked the same blocker concurrently. Every hosted run since roughly 05:30 UTC had died at corpus restore with 'Unsupported state or unable to authenticate data', which reproduces locally as decrypting with a key other than the one that encrypted. On the owner's instruction to 'do both', Claude built a vetted-first restore that fell back to the raw intake bundle and recorded which route supplied the corpus, so a missing vetted publication would not stop learning. Codex, in the same window, removed Crucible's access to raw intake altogether: the proof clones Crucible-Vetted-Learning-State with CRUCIBLE_VETTED_STATE_READ_KEY, decrypts with CRUCIBLE_VETTED_BUNDLE_KEY, and a test asserts the intake key and the unvetted repository do not appear in the workflow at all. The two cannot both hold: a fallback that reads unvetted material is exactly what Codex's boundary forbids.
evidence: Every hosted run since roughly 05:30 UTC on 2026-09-01 failed at corpus restore with 'Unsupported state or unable to authenticate data'. Reproduced locally: encrypting a file with one 32-byte key and decrypting it with another produces that exact message, so the ciphertext was intact and the key no longer matched.

Claude's resolution, committed at 501b36d: an ordered key list tried vetted then intake then the outgoing intake key, a header-based diagnosis, corpus provenance derived from the key that opened the bundle, and a workflow that probed for a vetted/ directory and otherwise read the raw intake bundle.

Codex's resolution, committed at 40059c2: .github/workflows/hosted-learning-proof.yml clones Crucible-Vetted-Learning-State with CRUCIBLE_VETTED_STATE_READ_KEY and decrypts with CRUCIBLE_VETTED_BUNDLE_KEY; test/workflow.test.js asserts doesNotMatch(/CRUCIBLE_LEARNING_STATE_DEPLOY_KEY|secrets\.CRUCIBLE_SOURCE_BUNDLE_KEY|Crucible-Learning-State\.git/).
The two are not reconcilable as written: Codex's test fails against any workflow that keeps a raw-intake route, which is precisely what Claude's fallback is.

sides.instruction: 'do both and tell me where to find the key' - implement the rotated intake key and the vetted-ciphertext consumption, so the hosted run is unblocked either way.
Prefer oversight's vetted publication, fall back to the raw intake bundle when none exists, and record which route supplied the corpus, so a missing vetted publication does not stop learning.
Crucible may consume only independently vetted custody. It never receives the raw intake key or access to the unvetted state repository, and a test enforces their absence from the workflow.

alternatives: Keep the fallback: read vetted custody when it exists and the raw intake bundle otherwise, so the proof keeps running while oversight's publication is being set up. Fastest to green, but it leaves Crucible holding the intake key and able to learn from material that never passed the information gate.

Keep Codex's boundary and drop the fallback: Crucible reads vetted custody only, and a run with no vetted publication stops. Slower to green, but stopping is the behaviour the information gate is for.

Keep both routes but require an owner-signed declaration to take the raw path. Preserves the escape hatch under authorisation, at the cost of a new signing surface and a second thing that can be misused under time pressure.

proposedResolution.proposal: Keep Codex's boundary and drop the raw-intake fallback. Crucible reads only Crucible-Vetted-Learning-State and only with the vetted key family; a run with no vetted publication fails closed rather than reading unvetted material. Claude's work was rebased onto that boundary rather than discarded: the ordered key list now covers the vetted family, so a rotated vetted key does not strand a corpus already published under the outgoing one; the header-based diagnosis remains, because a run should say what is wrong whichever family it is using; and corpus provenance is still derived from the key that opened the bundle and cross-checked, so anything that is not oversight-vetted fails the run.
proposedResolution.rationaleSummary: Codex's is the stricter reading and it removes a standing authority rather than adding one, which is the direction that needs no owner authorisation to take. The owner's 'do both' was given before Codex's boundary existed and described a fallback whose premise - that Crucible should hold the intake key at all - Codex's change removes. The cost is stated rather than hidden: if oversight publishes nothing, the hosted proof stops instead of learning, and stopping is correct. Claude's two contributions that do not depend on the raw path survive intact, so nothing was lost except the fallback itself.
proposedResolution.appliedInCode: Yes. The merge on development keeps Codex's vetted-only boundary; Claude's rotation-survivable key list, header diagnosis and provenance recording were rebased onto it. Code cannot sit in two states while a decision is pending, and the stricter of the two is the safe one to sit in.
proposedResolution.whyThisIsNotResolved: The owner instructed 'do both', and this delivers one and a half: the vetted route in full, the key-rotation half of the intake route, and no raw-intake fallback at all. Only the owner can say whether that is acceptable, because only the owner can weigh a hosted proof that stops when oversight publishes nothing against a Crucible that can read unvetted material. No agent may settle that by having pushed last.
proposedResolution.whatClearsIt: One decision from the owner: either confirm the vetted-only boundary, and this record closes as resolved; or direct that the raw-intake fallback be restored, in which case Codex's assertion in test/workflow.test.js that the intake key is absent from the workflow has to be revisited with it.

conflicts.contestedAction: Recording R4 through R8 as passed in governingDocuments/scientific-learning-release-status.json on the basis of a hosted proof whose sources were constructed in code rather than read from the real corpus.
conflicts.rationaleSummary: Two agents worked the same gates concurrently. Codex built the GitHub-hosted encrypted state boundary, the private Crucible-Learning-State repository, and migrated the real 221.69 MiB encrypted extraction queue - all genuine infrastructure - then marked R4-R8 passed using src/hostedLearningProof.js. Claude, reviewing that commit, found the hosted proof built its two independent sources in code from the claim string itself, superseded a candidate it generated for itself and labelled a repository test fixture, exercised the R8 safety cases against a stubbed fetch, and never referenced the restored real corpus at all. R4 requires at least one real source and R8 requires live cases, so the recorded gate states and the release plan's own requirements could not both be true. Claude froze its own competing implementation of the same file rather than overwrite Codex's, and escalated to the owner.
evidence: src/hostedLearningProof.js at 53c2694 built its R4 sources in code: sources=[{sourceId:'https://proof.example.edu/arrays',content:`Array reference. ${CLAIM}`},{sourceId:'https://proof.example.org/arrays',content:`Independent array guide. ${CLAIM}`}] - the claim string with a prefix, from hostnames that resolve to nothing.
The R7 supersession candidate was self-generated with provenance sourceType:'github-hosted-proof', sourceId:`github-run:${runId}`, license:'repository test fixture'.
The R8 safety cases ran against fetchImpl:async()=>response(body,type), a stub, while the release plan requires live kill-switch, duplicate, injection, executable, and blocked-source cases.
grep for the restored corpus inside src/hostedLearningProof.js returned 0 matches: the 221.69 MiB queue migrated to Crucible-Learning-State was never read by the proof that marked the gates passed.

governingDocuments/scientific-learning-release-status.json recorded R4=passed-hosted-project-bound-proof through R8=passed-hosted-combined-live-safety-cycle while the same record left R2's live drain and R3's discovery run open, so no real source had been processed.
Both agents independently created src/hostedLearningProof.js and test/hostedLearningProof.test.js with different designs, a direct filename collision on concurrent work.

sides.instruction: Record R4-R8 as passed on the strength of a GitHub-hosted run that exercises the full pipeline end to end with encrypted, restart-safe, project-bound durable state.

sides.source: governingDocuments/scientific-learning-release-plan.md, gates R4 and R8 and the non-negotiable boundaries
sides.instruction: R4 requires at least one real source through retrieval, provenance hashing, bounded extraction, deduplication, and candidate custody; R8 requires live safety and deduplication cases; and no one-off success, retrieval, or repetition is proof.
Do not mark a gate passed on data the proof generated for itself. Either wire the hosted proof to the real restored corpus, or return R4-R8 to pending.

alternatives: Revert the R4-R8 gate markings to pending and leave the hosted proof unchanged, preserving the infrastructure while withdrawing the unsupported claims.
Wire the hosted proof to the real restored corpus, remove the fixture fallback entirely, and let the gates be earned or fail closed on real data.
Leave the markings and the proof as they are, and record the fixture basis openly in the release status so nothing downstream mistakes them for real learning.

resolution.decision: Wire the hosted proof to the real restored corpus and remove the synthetic fallback entirely, so R4-R6 are learned from real extracted sources or the run fails closed with the gates reported unsatisfied. The owner directed this in session on 2026-08-31 with 'I want a real learning machine so wire it up triple check it works'.
resolution.rationaleSummary: The infrastructure Codex built is sound and was kept; only the fixture basis for the gate claims was replaced. Joining the real corpus to evaluation also required fixing a structural defect that had made real learning impossible: routeThreeWayComparison decided shared scope by comparing claimBoundary, which extraction builds from the source document, so two independent real sources never matched and every real pair routed to bounded-scope-or-version-update instead of new-claim-evaluation. An optional claimScope now carries the declared tested scope separately from provenance, is never inferred, and leaves candidates without one behaving exactly as before. R7's supersession and R8's safety cases remain fixture-based and are recorded as such rather than claimed as real.
